questions.question: What does `del x` do in CPython?
options: Immediately destroys the object x refers to, even if other references exist
Removes the name binding x and decrements the object's reference count
Moves the object to the oldest garbage collector generation
questions.explanation: del removes a name binding. The object is freed only when its reference count reaches zero (or the cycle collector reclaims it).

questions.question: Why does CPython need a cyclic garbage collector in addition to reference counting?
options: Reference counting is too slow to be used for most objects
Reference counting only works for immutable objects
The GIL prevents reference counts from being updated
Objects in a reference cycle keep each other's counts above zero even when unreachable
questions.explanation: Cycles (a refers to b, b refers to a) never reach a count of zero on their own, so the generational gc module detects and frees them.

questions.question: What does `sys.getsizeof(my_list)` report?
options: Only the memory of the list object itself, not the objects it contains
The total memory of the list and every object it references
The number of elements in the list
The peak memory used by the program so far
questions.explanation: getsizeof is shallow; referenced objects are not included. Walk the contents or use tracemalloc for a true footprint.

questions.question: Which change most reduces peak memory when summing the squares of 10 million numbers?
options: Using sum([n * n for n in range(10_000_000)])
Storing the squares in a dict first
Using a generator expression: sum(n * n for n in range(10_000_000))
questions.explanation: A generator expression yields one value at a time, so memory stays constant; the list comprehension materialises all 10 million results first.
